newsitem.title: USA: Generals say all nuclear arms should be scrapped.
newsitem.headline: Generals say all nuclear arms should be scrapped.

text.p: Two former top U.S. military commanders, one of whom would have had charge of launching nuclear missiles in wartime, called on Wednesday for the ultimate elimination of nuclear weapons on Earth.

Retired Air Force General Lee Butler, who was commander of U.S. nuclear forces until two years ago, and retired Army General Andrew Goodpaster, who was NATO's commander from 1969 to 1974, said the process should begin now with deep cuts.

"The ultimate objective of phased reductions must be the complete elimination of nuclear weapons from all nations. No one can say today whether or when this final goal will prove feasible," they said in a statement released to reporters.

The two former generals said complete elimination of the world's nuclear weapons would probably take decades but the United States and Russia should take the lead in reducing weapons numbers to "very low levels."
Sixty former military commanders from nations around the world, including Russia, planned a similar call on Thursday.

The White House, asked its response, said the generals' ideas have merit and the administration has followed the type of "step-by-step approach" they want. But it also made clear the U.S. nuclear deterrent will not soon be dismantled.

"We continue to believe that nuclear weapons will be part of the cornerstone of our current strategy for some time into the future. So there is not of course a complete agreement between us and the generals," spokesman David Johnson added.
Butler said in a separate statement that his experience commanding the nuclear arsenal convinced him that the risk of nuclear holocaust must be eliminated by scrapping the weapons.
"I have spent years studying nuclear weapons effects," he said. "I have investigated a distressing array of accidents and incidents involving strategic weapons and forces."

"I came away from that experience deeply troubled by what I see as the burden of building and maintaining nuclear arsenals ... The grotesquely destructive war plans, the daily operational risks, and the constant prospect of a crisis that would hold the fate of entire societies at risk."

Goodpaster and Butler said the need for nuclear weapons is almost gone with the end of the Cold War but the risk of keeping them is high because they could fall into the hands of terrorists or be launched accidentally.

They said in the joint statement that nuclear powers led by Washington and Moscow should not only cut their nuclear warheads to low numbers but remove them from alert status and put them in controlled storage.

President Bill Clinton's administration has said it will not cut U.S. nuclear weapons below the 6,000 already agreed upon until Russia's Duma, or parliament, approves a second Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty to cut them to about 3,500. It has suggested it would be willing to talk about cuts below 3,500 only after that number is formally approved.

Talking with reporters, Butler conceded that outlawing nuclear weapons would mean only terrorists and tyrants could build them and said "that may well be the new nuclear nightmare of the next century."

But he said maintenance of nuclear arsenals by current nuclear powers cannot prevent that. He said part of the answer is that the major powers ensure that any nation or group that uses a nuclear weapon would be destroyed by non-nuclear means.
